name: Caro-Kann Panov Attack
summary: The Panov Attack, 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4, hits the Caro-Kann with an aggressive isolated-queen's-pawn fight.
intro: The Caro-Kann Panov Attack arises after 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4, when White follows the exchange on d5 by striking at the centre with the c-pawn. The typical continuation 4...Nf6 5.Nc3 e6 transposes into an isolated queen's pawn structure with a distinctly Queen's-Gambit flavour, trading the quiet reputation of the Caro-Kann for open lines and active pieces. It is White's most combative way to meet the defence, offering attacking chances around the IQP against Black's aim of a secure blockade and a favourable endgame.
line: e4 c6 d4 d5 exd5 cxd5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: After 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 White immediately challenges Black's d5-pawn, and once the tension is resolved the game revolves around an isolated queen's pawn — usually White's d4-pawn after ...dxc4, or a hanging-pawns and IQP complex depending on the exact captures. These are the classic structures of the Queen's Gambit and Nimzo-Indian rather than of a typical Caro-Kann, so understanding the isolated pawn is far more important than memorising forcing lines. White's trumps are freer development, the two half-open files, and the outpost squares e5 and c5 for the pieces.

The strategic battle is the eternal one of the IQP. White uses the extra space and piece activity to build a kingside or central attack, often placing a knight on e5, a bishop on the b1-h7 diagonal, and rooks on the c- and e-files to hit e6 and d5. Black, in turn, welcomes exchanges of minor pieces, blockades the isolated pawn firmly on d5, and looks to steer the game toward an endgame where the isolated pawn becomes a lasting weakness rather than a source of energy. Timing determines everything: White must attack before Black consolidates, Black must trade and blockade before White breaks through.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: In the main line 4...Nf6 5.Nc3 e6 Black develops soundly and prepares ...Be7 and ...O-O, when White continues with Nf3, Bd3 or c4-c5 ideas and typical IQP piece play. A major alternative for Black is the fianchetto plan with 5...g6, developing the bishop to g7 to bear down on d4 and the long diagonal, a solid setup that invites structural rather than tactical battles. White frequently meets the classical setup by castling short, centralising the rooks, and preparing the d4-d5 break or a kingside pawn storm.

White has independent tries too, most notably the sharp 5.Nc3 Nc6 lines and the aggressive 6.Bg5 pinning the f6-knight to pressure d5 immediately. Black's most reliable path is to develop with ...Be7 or ...Bb4, castle quickly, and contest the centre with well-timed exchanges, keeping the d5-square under firm control. Because so many transpositions lead to Queen's Gambit Declined and Tarrasch structures, both sides draw on that broader body of isolated-pawn theory rather than on Caro-Kann-specific ideas.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The variation is named for Vasily Panov and Mikhail Botvinnik, Soviet masters who developed and popularised the plan of meeting the Caro-Kann exchange with an early c4 in the 1930s. Its appeal was clear: instead of the placid symmetry of the ordinary Exchange, White obtains the dynamic isolated-pawn positions that Botvinnik in particular understood deeply. The Panov-Botvinnik Attack has remained a respected mainstream weapon ever since, valued precisely because it forces Caro-Kann players onto the more open, initiative-driven terrain of the Queen's Gambit, and it endures as the principal aggressive antidote to the defence's solid structures.

keyIdeas: 4.c4 turns the Caro-Kann exchange into an isolated-queen's-pawn game.
Structures resemble the Queen's Gambit far more than a normal Caro-Kann.
White seeks piece activity, the e5 outpost, and a central or kingside attack.
Black blockades d5, trades pieces, and aims for a favourable endgame.
The 6.Bg5 pin adds immediate pressure to Black's d5-pawn.
Timing decides the fight: attack before consolidation, or blockade before the break.

white: Play c4 and Nc3 to pressure d5 and open the position quickly.
Develop actively with Bd3, Nf3 and a knight to e5.
Pin the f6-knight with Bg5 to intensify pressure on d5.
Attack on the kingside or prepare the d4-d5 central break.
Occupy the c- and e-files with rooks to hit e6 and d5.
black: Develop with ...Nf6, ...e6, ...Be7 and castle to a safe king.
Blockade the isolated pawn firmly on the d5-square.
Trade minor pieces to reduce White's attacking potential.
Adopt the ...g6 fianchetto to bear down on d4 and the long diagonal.
Steer toward an endgame where the isolated pawn is a weakness.
